name: Aaron Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at five checking the orders. We grow lettuce, broccoli and leeks on about ninety hectares at Fenside, and most of it goes to two supermarkets through a packer. By six the crew is in the field, twenty-five people in summer, and I'm between the field and the packhouse all day with my phone. My wife Grace teaches at the primary school, and our two girls are eleven and eight. What I love is a perfect field of lettuce at dawn, every head the same size. What wears me out is a supermarket changing an order at nine at night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you're on your phone all day. What for?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Orders, weather, and I use an AI assistant all day long. It reads the supermarket's forecast and helps me plan which field to cut. It also helps with the spray records and the worker rotas. My dad thought farming was muscle and weather, and it still is, but now it's also about who reads the numbers fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a fine tool, and any farmer not using it is leaving money on the table. I'd say that at the growers' association, and some of them would grumble. I'm used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, I want it to do more. But it's steady, and steady is good for a family with a mortgage. The real fight is still with the supermarkets on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it every day and try to get the packer to share their data with me, so the tools can plan better. I'd buy a second-hand cooling unit for the packhouse, about fifteen thousand, which we need either way. And I'd keep hiring my crew the same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little impatient, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the supermarket changing an order at nine at night.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last June they cut a lettuce order by a third at nine o'clock, after we'd cut it. Eight thousand heads in the cold store, and nowhere to send them. I spent till midnight ringing wholesalers and sold half at cost, the rest went to the pigs on my neighbour's farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do any of your crew use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My foreman, Tomasz, does now, I showed him. He uses it to translate safety instructions into four languages for the team. That alone has saved us a lot of confusion, and maybe a cut finger or two.

S0.say: It's a fine tool, and any farmer not using it is leaving money on the table. Some at the growers' association would grumble, but I'm used to it.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I want it to do more. But steady is good for a family with a mortgage, and the real fight is still with the supermarkets.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily and asks the packer to share data so his planning improves. Buys a second-hand cooling unit for the packhouse for about fifteen thousand and keeps hiring the crew as usual.
S0.quote: Eight thousand heads in the cold store, and nowhere to send them.
S0.fieldNote: He is confident and impatient for more from the tools, unusual for a traditional voter. His real battle is with the supermarkets, shown by the late-night order cut. His foreman using AI to translate safety instructions was a practical, human example.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and businesses should take on apprentices rather than wait for the government. I'd take on two myself. Hard work and a skill, that's what gets a young person on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, slow is good for me, I'm ahead of most growers and I'd stay ahead. The beginners bit worries me for the packhouse, because that's where young people from town start. If I hire fewer, I'm part of the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a proper apprenticeship for two school leavers, one in the field and one in the packhouse, paying the going rate plus training. I'd ask the church youth group if anyone was interested. And I'd keep investing in the planning tools, maybe a few hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of responsibility sitting on my shoulders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the church youth group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know the families, and they know me. If a lad from there doesn't turn up, his mother hears about it before I do. That kind of community is worth more than any job website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stay ahead, but worry about being part of the problem. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't completely. A business has to make money or there are no jobs at all. But a business that makes money and trains nobody is just taking, and I wasn't brought up to take.

S1.say: Ten years is plenty of time, and businesses should take on apprentices instead of waiting for the government. Hard work and a skill are what get a young person on.
S1.think: A slow change is good for me because I'd stay ahead of most growers. But the packhouse is where young people from town start, and if I hire fewer, I'm part of the problem.
S1.do: Starts a paid apprenticeship for two school leavers, one in the field and one in the packhouse, recruited through the church youth group. Keeps spending a few hundred a month on planning tools.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a sense of responsibility on his shoulders.
S1.quote: A business that makes money and trains nobody is just taking, and I wasn't brought up to take.
S1.fieldNote: His free-market views come with a strong sense of duty, rooted in faith and upbringing. He admitted he can't fully square staying ahead with hiring fewer beginners. He'd recruit through his church, where families hold young people to account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and people should get ready, not wait for politicians to argue it out. I'd say the government should make it easier to start a business and to train, not just hand out money. I'd post something like that and get a fair bit of argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the supermarket buying offices would go automatic, and their computers would squeeze me on every order. But I'd have the same tools, and I'm quicker than most growers, so I might do better than the slow ones. Grace's school might lose office staff, though, and she'd be doing their work on top of her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever ordering system the supermarkets bring in, first, so I learn it before the others. I'd look at taking on a part-time data person, maybe one of the laid-off office workers from town, to help me read the numbers. And I'd keep five months of savings and not dip into them for the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but ready. Like a match where you know the other side's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really hire a laid-off office worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if they were willing to get muddy now and then. Someone who's spent twenty years doing accounts would be worth gold to me. I'd pay them fairly, but they'd have to come to the field once a week to see what the numbers mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace about her extra work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say tell them no, which she won't. She's the kind who stays late every night already. So I'd do more of the school runs and the cooking, which my mother would find very funny.

S2.say: Change is coming and people should get ready, not wait for politicians. The government should make it easier to start a business and to train, not just hand out money.
S2.think: Supermarket computers would squeeze me on every order, but I'm quicker than most growers and might come out ahead. Grace's school might lose office staff, leaving her with their work.
S2.do: Signs up first to the supermarkets' new ordering system and hires a laid-off office worker part-time to read the numbers. Keeps five months of savings away from the business and takes on more school runs and cooking.
S2.feel: Anxious but ready, like facing a strong team in a match.
S2.quote: Someone who's spent twenty years doing accounts would be worth gold to me.
S2.fieldNote: He saw the change as a race he could win by moving first. He was the only one to plan hiring an office worker as a data helper, with a weekly trip to the field to keep them grounded. His home life showed too: more cooking and school runs to support his wife.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built it earned it, and we shouldn't punish them, but the country needs a fair deal so families aren't wrecked. I'd want any money spent on training and on helping people start businesses. Not on keeping people idle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, vegetables are physical and we'd be fine for now. People still eat broccoli. But a lot of unemployed office workers buy cheaper food, and the supermarkets would push the price down to keep them, and that comes straight out of my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut costs where I could, using the tools to plan cutting so less goes to waste. I'd look at a direct contract with a local restaurant chain, as a second customer, so I'm not only with the supermarkets. And I'd fix the mortgage before rates move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Safe for now, but I can see the squeeze coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your girls about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to work hard, learn to use the tools, and never forget how to do something with their hands. My eldest, Joy, wants to be a doctor. I'd say, be the doctor patients trust, because the computer can know things, but it can't sit and hold an old man's hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want money for training, not idleness. What about people who can't retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There'll be some, and I'd want them looked after, by their families and churches first, then the government if they've got nobody. I'm not cold about it. I just think work gives a person dignity, more than a cheque does.

S3.say: The people who built it earned it and shouldn't be punished, but families shouldn't be wrecked either. Spend the money on training and new businesses, not on keeping people idle.
S3.think: People still eat broccoli, so we're fine for now. But out-of-work office staff buy cheaper food, and the supermarkets would push my price down to keep them.
S3.do: Uses the tools to plan cutting and reduce waste, and seeks a direct contract with a local restaurant chain as a second customer. Fixes the mortgage before rates move.
S3.feel: Uneasy: safe for now but able to see the squeeze coming.
S3.quote: The computer can know things, but it can't sit and hold an old man's hand.
S3.fieldNote: He tied his price risk to the spending of unemployed office workers, through the supermarkets. When pressed on people who can't retrain, he softened: family and church first, then government. His advice to his daughter about becoming a trusted doctor was striking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest change farming has seen since the tractor, and the farmers who move first will survive. I'd say government should stay out of the way and let farms buy what they need. And I'd say we owe our workers a fair chance to move with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd go all in. Harvesting robots for lettuce and broccoli would fix my worst problem, which is finding twenty-five people every summer. But I'd be lying if I said I wasn't worried about my crew, some of them have been with me eight years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lease two harvesting robots in the first year, maybe forty thousand a year between them, and run them alongside the crew to see what they can really do. I'd train Tomasz and a few others to run and fix them, and pay them more for it. And I'd sit with the rest of the crew and be honest about what's coming, and help them find other work if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and excited together. It's a chance and a cliff edge at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the crew members you couldn't keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I'm sorry, and here's a reference and here's who's hiring. I'd ring round the other farms myself. Some of them pray with me on Sundays, I can't just look away from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said government should stay out of the way. Would you want help for your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training help, yes, I'd take that. I don't want a big scheme that keeps them at home. I want them on a course, learning to fix the robots that replaced them, if that's not too bitter a joke.

S4.say: This is the biggest change in farming since the tractor, and farmers who move first will survive. Government should stay out of the way, but we owe our workers a fair chance to move with us.
S4.think: Harvesting robots would fix my worst problem, finding twenty-five people every summer. But I'm worried about my crew, some of whom have been with me eight years.
S4.do: Leases two harvesting robots for about forty thousand a year and runs them alongside the crew. Trains Tomasz and others to run and fix them for higher pay, and helps the rest find other work, ringing round farms himself.
S4.feel: Alarmed and excited together, a chance and a cliff edge at once.
S4.quote: Some of them pray with me on Sundays, I can't just look away from them.
S4.fieldNote: He'd move first and fast, but the people he might let go are fellow churchgoers, which made it personal. He accepts training help from government but not schemes that keep people at home. His bitter joke about workers fixing the robots that replaced them showed he feels the cost.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because it's my crew on the line, even if it's good for the farm. What would help is training money for farm workers to learn to run and repair the machines, and fair rules so the supermarkets can't just squeeze every saving out of us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask farmers what they owe, not just what they're owed. We take from the land and from our workers. If the robots come, we have to give something back, or we've lost more than jobs.

headlineQuote: Some of them pray with me on Sundays, I can't just look away from them.
portrait: Aaron is a 43-year-old vegetable grower on ninety hectares at Fenside, supplying lettuce, broccoli and leeks to supermarkets, married to Grace, a primary school teacher. He uses AI all day, likes to move first and holds free-market, faith-centred views about work, family and church. Across the scenarios he sees a race he can win, but keeps returning to what he owes his crew and young people in town. In the robot scenario he'd lease harvesters straight away while feeling the weight of letting go workers he prays beside on Sundays.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because harvesting robots would help the farm but put his long-serving crew on the line.
whatWouldHelp: Training money so farm workers can learn to run and repair the machines, and fair rules stopping supermarkets from squeezing every saving out of growers.
